prompt:
Your ETL job de-duplicates 200,000 records with this function and takes minutes. Most records are distinct. What is the complexity, in terms of the number of records n, and what is the best fix?

```python
def unique(items):
    # Keep prior values in a list.
    seen = []
    out = []
    for x in items:
        if x not in seen:
            seen.append(x)
            out.append(x)
    # Preserve first-occurrence order.
    return out
```

Assume hashable records with constant-cost hashing and equality.

options.text: Θ(n); the slowness is Python overhead, so rewrite it in C
options.explanation: The function is not linear. `x not in seen` scans the whole list each time, so a C rewrite would still be quadratic, just with a smaller constant.

options.text: Θ(n log n); sort the items first
options.explanation: Nothing here sorts or halves anything. Sorting would make it Θ(n log n), but that is a fix, not the current cost, and it would lose the original order. Here n is the input item count.

options.text: Θ(n^2); make `seen` a set so the membership test is O(1) on average
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct inputs make the remembered list grow, and each membership check rescans it. A set gives expected constant-time membership under the hashing model, making the whole scan expected linear time.

options.text: Θ(n^2); replace the list `out` with a deque
options.explanation: `out.append` is already O(1) amortised. The quadratic cost comes from the membership scan on `seen`, not from building `out`.

workedExample: On distinct input, seen grows after every record, and list membership rescans it. Those increasing scans give quadratic work. Keep out as an ordered list but replace seen with a set and append to it with add. Under constant-cost hashing/equality and suitable hash distribution, total expected work becomes linear while preserving first-occurrence order.

prompt: Naive recursive Fibonacci computes each smaller result again whenever it is requested. What change explains the main benefit of memoisation?

options.text: It makes both recursive children run in parallel
options.explanation: Caching does not introduce parallel execution.

options.text: It makes Python integer addition constant-time at every size
options.explanation: Large integer additions still depend on bit length.

options.text: It reuses completed subproblem answers instead of recomputing them
options.explanation: Correct. Only a linear number of distinct arguments need to be evaluated.

options.text: It removes the first recursive descent to the base case
options.explanation: A cold cache has no answers yet, so the initial descent remains.

workedExample: Look for the same argument appearing in different branches. Memoisation saves its completed answer and returns that result on later requests. This removes exponential repetition, giving linearly many distinct computations, but it does not eliminate stack depth or growing-integer costs.

prompt: For a CPython list `lst` of length n, which operations take **Θ(n)** time, that is time growing in proportion to n? Use amortised cost for end pop (`lst.pop()`) and worst-case cost for the other operations. Select all that apply. Assume constant-cost equality comparisons.

options.explanation: Correct. Membership on a list is a linear scan; the worst case (absent or last) checks all n items.
Removing the last element needs no shifting and is amortised O(1); an occasional shrinking reallocation can cost O(n). Here n is the input item count.
Correct. Removing the first element shifts every remaining element left by one slot.
Not Θ(n). A list is an array of pointers, so indexing anywhere is O(1). Here n is the input item count.
Correct. A slice creates a new list and copies every pointer in the range, so a full slice is Θ(n). Here n is the input item count.

workedExample: Ask whether the operation visits or shifts many slots. Worst-case membership scans the list, front removal shifts the remainder and a full slice copies references. Indexing reaches one slot. End pop needs no shifting and has constant amortised cost, although resizing can make an individual call more expensive. Here n is list length and equality is assumed constant-cost.

options.text: Θ(log n), because it halves the list each call
options.explanation: There are only logarithmically many calls, but each copies the half it recurses on. Slicing is not free.

options.text: Θ(n log n), charging the original length on each call
options.explanation: Each call copies the chosen fraction of its shrinking input, rather than the original length. The successive halves add to about the original length.

options.text: Θ(n), because the shrinking slices sum to about the original length
options.explanation: Correct. Logarithmically many comparisons are swamped by copying. The geometric series of copied halves sums to less than the original list length.

options.text: Θ(1), because it may find the target at the first midpoint
options.explanation: That is the best case. In the worst case (target absent), it recurses all the way to an empty list.

workedExample: Halving limits recursion depth, but slicing copies the chosen range on each call. The successive copied halves have a linear total in original length n. That dominates the logarithmic comparisons. Pass index bounds instead to avoid allocation and restore logarithmic worst-case search under constant-cost comparisons.
